name: Pontos
note: The old sea, before Poseidon: Nereus, Phorkys, Keto

Nereus.note: The Old Man of the Sea: truthful, gentle, and unable to lie -- Herakles had to wrestle him through every shape he took to get directions to the Hesperides. Theog. 233-236

Thaumas.note: Wonder; father of the rainbow and the storm-winds both. Gives thaumaturge, a wonder-worker. Theog. 237

Phorkys.note: The old sea's crooked strength, father of monsters. Theog. 237

Keto.note: The sea-monster herself, mother of the Gorgons and the Graiai. Her name gives cetacean, the order of whales, and every ketos in Greek is a sea beast. Theog. 238

Eurybia.note: With a heart of flint, mother of the Titans Astraios, Pallas and Perses. Theog. 239

Iris.note: The rainbow, and the gods' messenger before Hermes. Gives iris (the eye's coloured ring and the flower), iridescent, iridium -- named for the colours its salts show. Theog. 265-266

Harpyiai.name: Harpyiai (Harpyiae)
Harpyiai.note: The snatchers -- Aello and Okypete, storm-winds in bird form, who stole Phineus' food until the sons of Boreas drove them off. Gives harpy. Theog. 265-269

Amphitrite.note: Queen of the sea and wife of Poseidon, counted among the fifty Nereids. Theog. 243, 930-933

Thetis.note: Silver-footed, mother of Achilles. Zeus and Poseidon both wanted her until Themis warned that her son would surpass his father, so they married her to a mortal -- and Achilles is the prophecy kept. Theog. 244, Il. 18.35-147

Galateia.note: The Nereid Polyphemos the Kyklops loved, and who loved Akis. Theog. 250, Ov. Met. 13.738-897

Psamathe.note: Mother of Phokos by Aiakos, whose murder by his half-brothers drove Peleus and Telamon out of Aigina. Theog. 260, Apollod. 3.12.6

Graiai.note: The Grey Ones, grey-haired from birth, who shared one eye and one tooth between three. Perseus stole the eye to make them tell him the way to the Gorgons. Theog. 270-273

Gorgones.note: Stheno, Euryale and Medousa -- the last alone mortal, and the one Perseus killed. Gives gorgon, and gorgonzola is not related however good the story would be. Theog. 274-283

Triton.note: Fish-tailed son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, who calms the sea by blowing on a conch. Gives triton the newt, and Neptune's largest moon. Theog. 930-933

unions.note: The Nereids are sea goddesses with no generation of their own; they are dated by the mortals they marry -- Thetis by Peleus, Psamathe by Aiakos -- so the distance from the Old Man of the Sea to the heroic age is carried here. Hesiod names all fifty; the tree keeps four.
Poseidon's bond to her is drawn across the eras: the Nereids sit twelve rows below their father and he does not. Theog. 930-933
Queen of the sea, whom he pursued to the ends of the water and won by a dolphin's argument. Theog. 930-933

Poseidon took Medousa in Athena's own temple, and Athena punished HER for it -- the snakes and the stone-turning stare are the punishment. Hesiod tells it as a meeting in a spring meadow; Ovid tells it as rape in the temple, and it is Ovid the tradition kept. Pegasos and Chrysaor sprang from her neck when Perseus struck her head off. Theog. 278-283; Ov. Met. 4.794-803
